facts.text: The opening card says this is based on a true story. It sort of is: co-writer Michael Ronald Ross once picked up a hitchhiking hippie named Donna who wouldn't leave his place.
The house Donna overstayed in was real: Ross was subleasing Harry Nilsson's Laurel Canyon home in 1969. She burned every spoon in the house cooking drugs.
Shot in about 13 days in October 1974, on a budget of roughly $150,000. The film then sat on the shelf until 1977.
Working titles included Weekend of Terror, Mrs. Manning's Weekend and Handful of Hours. On video in 1981 it became The Seducers.
Al Lettieri was first cast as George. He took a few thousand dollars in living expenses and vanished. Producers were advised not to chase him, since he was allegedly mob-connected.
The three stars were born exactly nine years apart: Seymour Cassel in 1935, Sondra Locke in 1944, Colleen Camp in 1953.
Sondra Locke was about 30 playing a teenager. Audiences reportedly laughed when her character claimed to be 17.
Cinematographer David Worth had to underexpose Locke's scenes to hide her crow's feet. She later said she appreciated his work.
The first editor-cinematographer was fired for bossing the director around. Locke recommended David Worth, who later credited this film for his whole career, including work with Clint Eastwood.
Production designer Jack Fisk's wife Sissy Spacek worked as a set dresser. A young Bill Paxton was also on the set decoration crew.
Seymour Cassel threatened to quit every day. After wrapping he refused to re-record dialogue, so editor David Worth dubbed George's voice, uncredited.
Locke said direction often amounted to 'break something' or 'eat something.' She and Cassel ended up directing their own performances, and Camp's.
A food-dumping scene dragged on so long that Cassel nearly punched director Peter S. Traynor. Traynor said he'd fight him anytime after the shoot.
Locke slapped the makeup man after days of snide comments. He tried to slap back, and the screaming match sent the crew running. He was fired.
Comedian Marty Allen was originally the grocery delivery man. His comic scene was cut, and Worth re-edited the footage of the women teasing him into their love scene.
The house was rented for $1,000 a week. Its owner was an L.A. menswear manufacturer who loved the idea of a movie shoot, and the crew trashed the place.
Colleen Camp is almost 10 years younger than Locke but plays a character of similar age. She was one of her earliest film roles.
The character Jackson was named after Jackson Browne. The writers had written his album liner notes while working at Capitol Records.
The first draft was titled Freak, a tribute to Tod Browning's Freaks. Writers were inspired by Polanski's Repulsion.
Clint Eastwood's Malpaso once developed this script, with Eastwood set to direct and Jack Lemmon as George. He said Jo Heims' rewrite was 'more Breezy than Misty' and passed.
The writers once rewrote the lead as an African-American role, titled Nigg, hoping for Richard Pryor. Pryor and Fred Williamson were both reportedly interested.
Production stalled when the SEC investigated director Traynor's financing. He had funded his movies through limited partnerships with California doctors.
MGM stepped in with $100,000 to finish the film and helped find distributor Levitt-Pickman. Editing took three weeks at 15 hours a day.
Locke's career-boosting turn in The Outlaw Josey Wales (1976) may be why the film got released at all, three years after it was shot.
The credited writers didn't know the film existed until a Writers Guild dispute with Jo Heims. Heims' draft wasn't used, and the writers won with their original drafts.
Traynor and Spiegel apparently bought the script thinking Jo Heims, who wrote Play Misty for Me, had written it.
Locke was dating Bo Hopkins during this shoot. She dumped him for Clint Eastwood in 1975, and they became one of Hollywood's best-known couples.
Scholar John Kenneth Muir reads a feminist theme into the film, noting the opening song 'Good Old Dad' and the women constantly calling George 'daddy.'
The score is by Jimmie Haskell. 'Good Old Dad' has lyrics by Iris Rainer, who also wrote Beaches.
Critic Leonard Maltin called it an 'unpleasant (and ultimately ludicrous) film.' Variety called it a 'grisly try at horror exploitation.'
It premiered April 13, 1977 in Colonie, New York, as a 'test market' release. Box office was reported as 'poor' to 'fair.'
Locke never liked the movie and was surprised it became a cult hit. She backed the idea of a remake shortly before she died.
Remade twice: the 1980 Spanish film Vicious and Nude, and Eli Roth's Knock Knock (2015) with Keanu Reeves. Traynor, Locke and Camp were executive producers on Knock Knock.
Camp also has a cameo in Knock Knock. Her Blu-ray commentary for this film is moderated by Eli Roth.
Grindhouse Releasing's 2-disc Blu-ray adds Little Miss Innocence (1973), the film this one is said to remake, plus a Locke phone interview.
The 2019 restoration was transferred from the original camera negative in widescreen. Earlier home video releases were letterboxed from poor elements.
Locke, Cassel and Traynor all died within a year of each other: Locke in November 2018, Cassel in April 2019, Traynor in October 2019.
Cassel and Traynor ran into each other years later at a movie theater and agreed to let bygones be bygones.
